sections.title: Situation
sections.prompt: What is the real decision, by when, and which numbers frame it?
criteria: Restates the decision as a team in seats in time for the month-6 back-to-school release, inside $3.6M, under one fair pay rule
Derives the VP Product's mix at market ($4.06M) and at band ($3.40M)
Derives the band acceptance rate (3 of 11, about 27%) and what it does to the calendar
States at least one thing out of scope

sections.title: Stakeholders
sections.prompt: Who has a stake, what does each want, and how do you bring them along?
criteria: Covers at least the CFO, HR or the comp committee, the VP Product and recruiting, each with a distinct want
Says what the VP Product gives up (a staff engineer, a head, a later triage date) and how it is agreed
Includes the 40 L5 engineers outside AI and the managers who lose transfers
Ends with one idea that ties the stakeholders together

sections.title: Options
sections.prompt: What are the real hiring and pay options, and how does each fare on budget, calendar and fairness?
criteria: Includes hiring at the standard bands (the do-nothing on pay) as an option
Rules out a premium for new hires only, citing the comp committee and the 40 L5 engineers
Shows that hiring at band leaves the team incomplete until about month 10
Compares options on one table with the same criteria

sections.title: Decision and Trade-offs
sections.prompt: What do you recommend, what do you give up, and what would make you change course?
criteria: Makes one clear recommendation with a level mix that fits inside $3.6M
Names what is given up, including the 12th head and the second staff engineer
Says whether the pay range and the level mix are reversible
Gives a dated revisit with measurable triggers

sections.title: Economics
sections.prompt: What does each option cost over three years, and what does a late team cost?
criteria: Compares 3-year run-rate cost for each option from the level mix
Prices the cost of a late team as deferred ARR ($500k a month)
Prices extending the AI range to all 40 L5 engineers ($2.4M a year) to show why it is scoped to the role
Labels the compensation figures as assumed and names who pays for transfer backfills

sections.title: Org and Ownership
sections.prompt: Who owns leveling, offers and the AI range?
criteria: Names who decides the level, separate from who negotiates the offer
Allocates the 11 or 12 people across the AI tutor, triage and shared work
Gives HR ownership of the AI range and its yearly review

sections.title: Plan and Milestones
sections.prompt: How do you get the team in seats before the back-to-school release?
criteria: Starts the 4 transfers in month 1 and the staff engineer search first
Shows the offer count and calendar for the external hires (about 10 offers, last start by month 5)
Has at least one gate with a measurable threshold
Includes the month-6 revisit of the 12th head

sections.title: Risk and Governance
sections.prompt: What could go wrong with fairness, leveling and the process itself?
criteria: Applies the same loop and the same bar to internal and external candidates
Writes down the AI role criteria so the range has a documented, job-based reason
Forbids up-leveling to close an offer, and says what flexibility is allowed instead
Has a fallback if offers are still declined at market

sections.title: Metrics
sections.prompt: How do you know the hiring plan worked, and what would show it is causing harm?
criteria: Pairs each success metric with a guard metric
Tracks offer acceptance against the 70% assumption
Tracks attrition among the L5 engineers outside AI as the internal-equity guard
Tracks run-rate cost against $3.6M

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: What does each audience hear, and how often?
criteria: Gives a one-line message for at least five audiences
Tells the wider engineering org how anyone can reach the AI range, before offers go out
Tells the VP Product exactly what is given up
Sets a cadence for hiring status
